title: Precipitation Characteristics & Missing Records
subtitle: Beyond just measuring rain, engineers need to characterise it — how intense is it? How often does it occur? Over what area? And what do you do when a gauge station has missing data? This week answers all of that.
learningOutcome: Beyond just measuring rain, engineers need to characterise it — how intense is it? How often does it occur? Over what area? And what do you do when a gauge station has missing data? This week answers all of that.

content.text: Rainfall intensity indicates the variation of precipitation with time. The result can be presented in the form of an intensity-duration graph.

items: This is the average time period within which a rainfall of specific amount or intensity can be expected to occur once. This is known as the "return period" or the re-occurrence interval.
Re-occurrence interval = the average number of years in which a given event will be equalled or exceeded.

This concerns the area over which a point's rainfall can be held to apply. Storm totals obviously vary considerably, so the scale of individual catchments determines its importance — for large systems (local thunderstorm, tropical disturbance or extra-tropical depression) and its rate of movement determines the areal extent.
The variation of intensity with time is described with the aid of an intensity-duration curve in which rainfall intensity in mm/hr is plotted against duration of rainfall in minutes.
For duration over 2 hours: i = c / t^n

content.text: i = average intensity (mm/hr) · T = return period (years) · t = duration of precipitation (minutes) · K, x, a, b, n = constants depending on locality

topics.title: Methods of Estimating Missing Rainfall Records

subtopics.title: Methods of Estimating Missing Rainfall Records

content.text: Sometimes a raingauge station breaks down or has gaps in its records. You need to estimate the missing data from surrounding stations. Two methods are used:

P_x = estimated daily precipitation volume at the missing data station x (depth) · P_A, P_B, P_C = estimated daily precipitation volume at the adjacent stations A, B, C (depth) · N_x = the normal annual precipitation at the missing data station · N_A, N_B, N_C = average annual precipitation at the adjacent stations A, B, C · n = number of surrounding stations used

items: Use Arithmetic Average procedure when the normal annual precipitations at A, B, C are within 10% of that for station X.
Use Normal Ratio method when the variation is more than 10%.
Check: if N_A/N_x, N_B/N_x, N_C/N_x are all within 1.145 (i.e. within 10%), use arithmetic average.

content.text: Common mistake — Always check the 10% rule BEFORE choosing a method. Students jump straight to the Normal Ratio formula without checking. If ALL surrounding stations are within 10% of N_x, the simple arithmetic average is sufficient and faster.
